text.p: Serbian economists criticised on Wednesday the new draft privatisation law as an illusion of reforms helping the rich get richer but incapable of healing the devastated economy.
Economics professor Jovan Rankovic said the concept did not take into account the key aim -- to keep companies working and surviving.

"Yugoslavia has 4,600 socially-owned companies employing 1.5 million people. They need up to 50 billion dinars ($8.97 billion) to return to 1989 production levels and raise capacity utilisation to around 80 percent," Rankovic said.
"They are all facing bankruptcy and if the state sells shares to workers at big discounts, there will be no money left for the companies to get back on their feet," he said.
Serbia presented on Monday its new draft privatisation law, refraining from voucher privatisation but envisaging a heavy 20 percent basic discount for employees and pensioners.
The government expected privatisation to begin as early as July and involve four million people.
But economists blamed the government for using an important reform law for its own political purposes in an election year.

"The government is well aware that privatisation is a must. Half of the total capital will be given to workers. It is a politically efficient move for the audience not educated on privatisation issues, who eye the move as a big step toward reforms," said one analyst .

Another analyst who spoke under condition of anonymity said: "Judging by the draft, 1997 will not be the year of reforms as announced by the government. This concept will lead to an even deeper gap between the rich and the poor."

Danilo Sukovic of the Institute of Social Science said privatisation will be neither quick nor efficient. "It relies on insider privatisation and others, including workers, cannot buy shares because most are penniless anyway."
Sukovic said privatisation law needed to be more radical and to include vouchers and management buy-outs.

"The law may be good but not in Yugoslavia and not now. It does not imply that the process will quickly create sufficient quantities of fresh capital to revive the economy," said Slobodan Milosavljevic of the Institute for Market Research.
Dispersed ownership was not seen bringing any good to the economy.

"Usually, privatisation aims at finding new owners with capital and knowledge to improve the company's performance. Workers have neither and that is the key defect of this law," Zoran Popov of the Economics Institute told Reuters.
Serbia said it planned to privatise companies worth 60 billion to 70 billion German marks.
The size of hard currency kept by the population outside the banking sector is unofficially estimated between three and six billion marks.

"If they are willing to invest two billion, and if two billion German marks are attracted from abroad, total demand would stand at four billion marks the most. Meanwhile, poor and penniless workers will be forced to sell their shares cheap to the management," an analyst said.

"This will give a chance to those who got rich over past several years to buy shares of the most promising companies at a price not exceeding 10-20 percent of the face value," said an analysts, insisting the concept was far from socially fair. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
